reading.title: After the Practice Quiz
reading.purpose: Listen as two eighth graders weigh honesty, loyalty, and responsibility.
paras: "Wait a second," Tariq said, stopping by the lockers after third period. "Did you see Sam snap a photo of the math review key when Mr. Ortiz stepped into the hall?"
"I saw," Priya replied, lowering her voice. "He sent it to our group chat. I deleted it right away, because using a stolen key is obviously not ethical."

"Same here," Tariq said, frowning. "Still, my conscience is bothering me. That quiet inner voice telling right from wrong will not let me pretend nothing happened. If we stay silent while half the table copies it, are we complicit—quietly involved in the wrongdoing even though we did not take the photo?"

Priya leaned against her locker and thought for a moment. "I do not think we are as culpable as Sam, since he actually took and shared the picture. Yet ethics is not just about avoiding trouble. It is about holding ourselves accountable, owning the results of what we choose to do—or ignore. Loyalty is a real virtue, a strong quality of character, except when it covers up something unfair. We cannot pretend we did not see it."

"What if I talk to Sam before lunch?" Tariq asked. "Not to lecture him, just to give him a chance to tell Mr. Ortiz himself. That gives him a way to atone, to own the mistake and repair the trust before Friday's test." Priya nodded. "That is a genuinely moral choice—and honestly, an altruistic one too, since you are helping Sam do the right thing without getting any reward for yourself. Come on, let us find him before fifth period."

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "complicit" most nearly means
choices: completely unaware that a classmate broke a school rule
involved in a wrongdoing alongside others, even indirectly
eager to earn a prize by reporting friends to a teacher
confused about which math problems will appear on a quiz
qs.why: Tariq defines complicit directly as "quietly involved in the wrongdoing even though we did not take the photo."

qs.q: Which sentence shows Priya explaining when loyalty stops being a good quality?
choices: Priya leaned against her locker and thought for a moment.
Yet ethics is not just about avoiding trouble.
It is about holding ourselves accountable, owning the results of what we choose to do—or ignore.
Loyalty is a real virtue, a strong quality of character, except when it covers up something unfair.
qs.why: This sentence names loyalty as a virtue and adds the exact limit: "except when it covers up something unfair."

ev.text: Loyalty is a real virtue, a strong quality of character, except when it covers up something unfair.

qs.q: Why does Tariq want to speak with Sam before going to Mr. Ortiz?
choices: He wants Sam to take responsibility and repair the mistake on his own first.
He hopes Sam will send him a clearer photo of the math review key.
He is afraid that Mr. Ortiz will cancel Friday's test for the whole grade.
He thinks Priya should be the only student who talks to the teacher.
qs.why: Tariq says talking to Sam gives him "a chance to tell Mr. Ortiz himself" so Sam can atone and rebuild trust.

qs.q: What is the main theme of this dialogue?
choices: Group chats should never be used to discuss homework or upcoming math tests.
Real integrity means taking responsibility and helping friends face mistakes honestly.
Students should never speak up about cheating unless a teacher asks them directly.
Deleting a stolen photo from your phone solves every moral problem automatically.
qs.why: Tariq and Priya move beyond simply deleting the photo, choosing an honest, principled step that encourages Sam to own up.
